title: Carrom: strike the striker from the base lines with a finger so it pockets the queen, without following it in
instruction: Pocket the red queen with one stroke: strike the striker, which lies on your base lines, so that it knocks the queen into a pocket, and do not let the striker follow it in. Strike the striker with your fingers, do not push it. Do not touch the queen, and do not touch the striker again once it has left the base lines.
context: Carrom is one of the most played table games in South Asia, in homes, clubs and cafes. Every shot is a bare-finger strike of the striker from the base lines: it must slide 0.63 m to within about 1 cm of its line, fast enough to send the queen in but slow enough that the striker does not follow (a foul), with no tool to guide it and no chance to correct.
setup: A full-size tournament carrom board (as in Surco's or Precise's ICF-approved Champion boards, about $185 to $250 with striker and carrom men): a plywood playing surface 74 cm square and 10 mm thick, dusted with carrom powder, its top 0.762 m above the floor on a four-legged stand, from x = 0.220 to 0.960 m and y = -0.370 to +0.370 m, in a rosewood frame 7 cm broad standing 2.2 cm above it. Four round corner pockets 4.45 cm across, centred 24.25 mm in from both sides of the frame, with a net under each. ICF markings: on each side two base lines 47 cm long (the outer one 10.15 cm from the frame, 6 mm thick; the inner one 3.18 cm from its outer edge), closed by base circles 3.18 cm across with red centres; four arrows; a centre circle 3.18 cm and an outer circle 17 cm across. Striker: a smooth dark blue disc 41.3 mm across, 9 mm thick, 15 g, lying on the robot's base lines touching both, centred at (0.3405, -0.0682) m. Queen: a red wooden carrom man 31.5 mm across, 8 mm thick, 5.5 g, centred at (0.8865, 0.3115) m, 6 cm short of the far left pocket's centre (0.9358, 0.3458) on the straight line from the striker. No other pieces. Two YAM arms on 750 mm pedestals at x = 0, y = +/-0.305 m, 40 N parallel grippers.
scoring: The trial scores 0 (a foul) if the robot touches the queen; if it is still touching the striker when the striker's centre is more than 1 cm off the base-line strip (a push); if it touches the striker again once the striker, untouched, has moved more than 1 cm off the strip (after the stroke); if either disc is ever more than 5 mm above the board with nothing touching it, or comes to lie on the frame or off the board; or if the board moves. The strip is where the striker's centre can be while it touches both base lines, between the base circles' centres. Otherwise the score is set once both discs are untouched and still (under 5 mm/s for 1 s) after the stroke: 1.0 the queen has dropped through a pocket and the striker has not; 0.5 both have dropped; 0.25 the queen has moved at least 1 cm from its spot and neither has dropped; 0 otherwise (a miss, no stroke, or the striker dropped alone).
reset_notes: Take the queen out of the net and set both discs back on their pencil-marked spots; brush powder lumps off the board. Before each set of trials, flick the striker across the board by hand and film it from above at 60 fps beside a tape measure: it must slow by 0.35 to 0.43 m/s each second (friction 0.04). Dust on carrom powder to make the board faster, or wipe some off to make it slower. Judge pushes on a 240 fps video beside the base lines.
fidelity: PhysX at 960 Hz, 20 Hz control. Board, pockets, markings and discs sized to the ICF laws. The powdered board is a uniform friction of 0.04 (published: 0.02-0.05), not loose grains; striker on queen restitution 0.82, frame rebound about 0.6. Discs are 48-sided prisms with 0.8 mm bevels; the corner squares and end strips sit 0.2 mm below the middle so discs do not catch on seams between collision shapes. Rigid nets; no air drag. Unmodified YAM arms; closed fingers strike in place of a fingernail.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (400 steps; never touched a disc); demo: 1.0 (scripted; the queen pocketed and the striker not, scored at step 166)
